title: The jam that wasn’t, and the joy that was
text:
The jam that wasn’t, and the joy that was
Things don’t always go as planned. Sometimes, they go better.
Dear family with the pear tree by the school:
Thank you for letting me harvest your pears again. You’re very generous. As always, I stood on the sidewalk nearest the fire station and collected only the pears I could reach with my fruit-picker pole.
As in past years, I’m leaving you a jar of jam with this note. It is not spiced pear jam, as you can see. It is strawberry jam. There is a reason for this, which I will get to.
But first: I have learned, finally, not to wait until ripe pears are splatting on the sidewalk before I ask your permission to pick. Now, I know that I need to begin about two weeks earlier, when the pears are “tree ripe.” They fully ripen in a few days if I set them on the dining room table.
This was a banner year for pears. I asked my wife if she wanted to come along this time. I typically need about 4 pounds of pears per batch of jam, times two or three batches, plus some for eating, and perhaps a few for pear muffins, made with pear nectar and cardamom.
Pears can be difficult to harvest. The tree is overgrown, and many of the pears are out of reach, even with an 8-foot pole. The sidewalk is a little elevated, though, which gives me about a 3-foot advantage.
Some years, the pears are small or misshapen or heavily insect-damaged. Sometimes, as in last year, there just aren’t very many of them. This year’s crop consisted of many large, remarkably unblemished, supermarket-quality pears. (And organic, too.) My theory is that sometimes the sheer quantity of fruit overwhelms the insects prepared to eat them. The bugs just can’t get to all of them. Fewer pears last year might have also meant fewer predators to eat this year’s crop.
It was a beautiful, sunny, late-summer afternoon in our New England town. The pears glowed yellow against the dark green leaves. Clusters of them hung well within reach of the orchard pole, which has a clawed wire basket to pull and catch the fruit. My wife, Maggie, and I set to work, taking turns with the picker, handling the fruit gently.
A mom stopped by – someone Maggie knew from town. She owns the bookstore. “Want a pear?” we asked. Of course she did. “We have permission,” I said.
Soon, several other moms stopped, and a man walking a dog. “Can I get you a pear?” Everyone who got a pear looked just a little jollier.
Wait, what was happening? Waves of moms and kids and strollers started coming toward us. School was out, and it was pickup time.
We couldn’t just arbitrarily stop giving out pears. But our generosity was outpacing the harvest.
“She has been asking me about those pears for weeks,” one mother confided. The little girl took the pear that we offered as though it – and her small hands – were magnetic. She was so focused and excited, she practically vibrated.
“Hey, guys! Keep up the good work!” said a man driving a pickup truck. “You’re the talk of the school!”
Word had traveled.
The stream of parents and children finally began to ebb. But we still had plenty of pears – all the pears we needed. We also had something else: A warmth in our hearts from sharing the bounty, which was actually the generous bounty of the tree’s owners – which is why I had to write this letter to you.
So why strawberry jam?
I’d made it earlier, with gifted West Coast berries provided by my oldest son and his wife-to-be. I had decided that pear jam could wait for some other projects, and I thought our harvest would be safe in the fridge.
But as I began to sterilize jam jars, I found I was too late. My precious pears had turned into green-brown, pear-shaped balloons filled with liquid.
Out they went to the compost heap. I’m sure the fruit flies and worms were grateful.
Losing the pears before they could be jammed was a disappointment. But my wife and I realized we were content. We had turned the pears into children’s smiles. That was more than enough.
I hope you agree. And I do hope you like strawberry jam.
